01 / THE BIGGER PICTURE+

Better technology. Stronger networks. More collaboration.

We invest in digital tools. But what helps people actually use them together?

Construction projects connect people, disciplines, and decisions. Digital tools can support those connections—but access to technology is only part of the story.

Our research extends the Theory of Planned Behavior to examine social network support. The colleagues who share advice, offer examples, and help solve problems may matter alongside individual beliefs.

Meet the network extension ↗
THE QUESTION THAT GUIDES US

Does access to supportive colleagues explain digital collaboration beyond individual attitudes, expectations, and perceived ability?

SUPPORTING RECORDS
How the map was built +

9,438 Scopus entries were consolidated into 8,885 unique records. A term-based construction-context screen retained 1,207; 7,678 were outside that scope. 155 records do not match the six themes and remain available in the literature panel. The collection combines 27 Scopus search exports, including overlapping and filtered results.

Screening uses construction-related terms in titles and keywords, or an explicit construction context in abstracts. It is not a full-text eligibility review: incidental matches may remain, and exclusions do not establish a literature gap.

The six themes group recurring terms in titles, abstracts, author keywords and indexed keywords. Membership is assigned by phrase matching rather than full-text interpretation of theories or findings. Each term occurs in at least 3 records. Case and hyphen variants are matched, and a record may belong to several themes.

Lines connect themes found in the same records. Each record counts once per theme pair. These links represent shared terminology, not citations, causality or shared findings.

The theme view shows up to 8 links supported by at least 3 shared records, ranked by Jaccard overlap (intersection / union). GAP shows all nonzero overlaps. Node positions aid reading rather than represent statistical distances; record counts do not measure the importance of a research field.

Author keywords and indexed keywords are shown separately. Matches from titles and abstracts retain their field labels. References and citation counts are not used to construct the map. Duplicate detection uses DOI, EID, or matching title, year and authors. Study findings were not assessed through full-text review.

THE RESEARCH GAP

Prior integration exists.

Prior research has connected behavioral explanations with social, relational, organizational, and enabling factors.

However, a more specific question remains.

THE UNRESOLVED QUESTION

Does practical support through project relationships add explanatory value beyond established TPB predictors in explaining digital collaboration behavior?

NE-TPB examines this question by incorporating relational access to practical support into the behavioral framework.

Here, network-informed refers to perceived access to practical support through project relationships rather than structural network measures.

Explore the gap

Prior construction research has applied behavioral theories to technology adoption, knowledge sharing, cooperation, and collaborative behavior, with some studies incorporating social, relational, organizational, and enabling factors. Less clear is whether access to practical support through project relationships adds explanatory value beyond established TPB predictors in explaining reported digital collaboration behavior. This study addresses that question through a network-informed extension of TPB.

Theme overlap provides context for the research question; it does not establish a theoretical gap. The findings present the empirical test.

FROMBehavioral intention alone→TOWARDBehavior embedded within project relationships

A shift in emphasis, building on prior research. Behavioral intention was not measured in this study.

Traditional TPB predictors Network extensionConceptual paths · associations, not causal effects

The study uses TPB-based predictors; behavioral intention was not measured. Project management experience is included as a control in the empirical analyses. The focused mediation SEM examines SNS, PBC, and DCF rather than the full conceptual model. Practice examples are illustrative paraphrases.

Outcome: self-reported collaboration frequency. Unadjusted R²; pp = percentage points. Source: manuscript, Table 5.

01

Support adds explanatory power.

Network support explains additional variance beyond attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control. Its association remains strong after controlling for experience.

02

Confidence is part of the pathway.

Perceived behavioral control statistically mediates 22.1% of the total SNS–DCF association in the bootstrap composite analysis. The direct association remains dominant.

03

Frequency is the outcome.

The findings describe how regularly people report collaborating with digital tools. They do not measure collaboration quality, effectiveness, or AI use alone.

THE CENTRAL IMPLICATION OF OUR RESEARCH

✳
04 / FROM RESEARCH TO PRACTICE+

Build the support. Enable the collaboration.

Practical directions for project teams, educators, and digital leaders.

↗
01 / CONNECT

Empower digital champions.

Identify approachable colleagues who can demonstrate tools, share examples, and offer help within everyday project work.

Put it into practice +

Make it clear who can help with common tools. Give champions time to assist colleagues, and recognize their contribution to team learning.

⌘
02 / EXCHANGE

Make knowledge sharing a routine.

Create space for short demonstrations, peer mentoring, and discussion of digital or AI-generated project information.

Put it into practice +

Bring one practical example to a regular team meeting: a useful workflow, a problem solved, or an output that needs collective review.

⊞
03 / ENABLE

Turn access into capability.

Pair tool provision with practical training, time to experiment, and clear channels for troubleshooting.

Put it into practice +

Use realistic project tasks in training. Offer a shared help channel and protected practice time so questions can become learning opportunities.

These are practice implications informed by observed associations, not interventions evaluated by this study.

05 / THE RESEARCH BEHIND THE RESULTS+

Transparent methods. Careful interpretation.

A quantitative, cross-sectional survey with hierarchical regression and a focused mediation structural equation model.

Explore the research materials ↗
01 Sample & measurement−

210 valid responses from construction professionals in a single-country, self-selected sample. Attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioral control, and social network support each use three items. DCF is a single frequency-oriented self-report item.

02 Analysis & robustness+

Hierarchical regression tests the incremental contribution of SNS, with HC3 robust standard errors. A focused mediation SEM examines the SNS–PBC–DCF pathway with experience as a control. Bootstrap composite mediation uses 20,000 resamples.

03 Boundaries & future research+

The design supports association, not temporal or causal ordering. Same-source self-reports, a single-item outcome, overlap in social construct wording, and sample composition limit interpretation. Future studies can use longitudinal, multi-country, and multilevel designs and objective use measures.
